pair.english: What would you like to drink?

response.english: Mint tea, if there is any.

pair.english: Do you want it sweet or bitter?

lessons.culture: Gulf coffee (gahwa) is lightly roasted Arabic coffee with cardamom, poured in tiny cups by the host, usually unsweetened and served with dates; you shake the cup gently to say you have had enough. In cafes, sweet milky karak chai is just as common an order.

too_formal.feedback: Bookish; murra alone does the job at a cafe.

exercises.tip: murra is 'bitter'. Gulf coffee (gahwa) is served unsweetened.

exercises.prompt: Which one asks a woman 'What do you want to drink?'

too_formal.feedback: MSA; in the Gulf you say shu tabeen with the -een ending for a woman.

exercises.tip: Man: tabi tishrab. Woman: tabeen tishrabeen.

too_formal.item: أرغب في فنجان قهوة من فضلك
too_formal.feedback: MSA; nobody orders like this at a table.

exercises.tip: law samaht (to a woman: law samahti) is the everyday please.

too_formal.feedback: MSA; Gulf speech says il7een for 'now'.

exercises.tip: il7een means 'now' in Gulf Arabic, not halla2 as in the Levant.

too_formal.feedback: Uses the MSA 'ma3a' and 'ureed'; the Gulf says abi and bil.

exercises.tip: bil is bi + al joined to the noun, no separate word for 'with'.

too_formal.feedback: Correct MSA but too long for a cafe order.

exercises.tip: wasa6 is 'middle': medium sugar.

exercises.prompt: Coffee with no sugar at all.

too_formal.feedback: Grammatically fine but nobody strings it together like this.

exercises.tip: abad at the end strengthens the negation: 'never/at all'.

too_formal.feedback: MSA 'ureed'; the Gulf uses abi (or abgha in Saudi).

exercises.tip: abi is 'I want' in the UAE and Kuwait.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: I like my coffee bitter.

too_formal.feedback: Too heavy; simple a7ibb ... murra is what you hear.

exercises.tip: murra comes last and describes the coffee.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: What do you want to drink?

too_formal.feedback: MSA; shu is the everyday 'what'.

exercises.tip: In Kuwait you may also hear shinu instead of shu.

dialogue.speaker: Rashid
dialogue.english: Welcome, here is the menu.

dialogue.speaker: Khalid
dialogue.english: Welcome to you too, do you have an English menu?

dialogue.speaker: Rashid
dialogue.english: Yes indeed, I'll bring it now.

dialogue.speaker: Rashid
dialogue.english: We have the dish of the day, chicken machboos.

dialogue.speaker: Khalid
dialogue.english: Good, what do you recommend I take with it?

dialogue.speaker: Rashid
dialogue.english: Take a salad and soup with it.

dialogue.speaker: Khalid
dialogue.english: Okay, and are there desserts?

dialogue.speaker: Rashid
dialogue.english: Sure, we have luqaimat and kunafa.

pair.english: Do you have an English menu?
What do you recommend I get?

response.english: Get the machboos, it's very good.
Yes, we have salads and vegetables.

lessons.culture: Restaurant menus in the UAE and Kuwait are almost always bilingual, and many staff speak English, Hindi or Urdu as well, so asking for an English menu is completely normal. Machboos (spiced rice with chicken or meat) is the classic Gulf dish, and luqaimat (fried sweet dumplings) is a favourite dessert.

exercises.prompt: Which one asks 'Do you have an English menu?'

too_formal.feedback: MSA; the word menu is used as it is.

exercises.tip: 3indkum literally 'at you (all)': the polite way to ask what a place has.

exercises.prompt: Which one means 'Is it spicy or not spicy?'

too_formal.item: هل هو حار أم غير حار؟
too_formal.feedback: MSA; ولا replaces أم and مو replaces غير.

exercises.tip: moo is the everyday 'not' in Kuwait; in the UAE you also hear mub.

exercises.prompt: حار ولا مو حار؟ (7aar walla moo 7aar?)

too_formal.feedback: MSA; the Gulf says waayid for 'very / a lot'.

exercises.tip: waayid is the classic Gulf word for 'very' and 'a lot'.

exercises.prompt: عندكم منيو بالإنجليزي؟ (3indkum menu bil inglizi?)

too_formal.feedback: Too stiff for a waiter; akeed, tfaddal is enough.

exercises.tip: tfaddal means 'here you are' when handing something over.

too_formal.feedback: MSA; the Gulf just says shu fii.

exercises.tip: hal- is the short form of hatha al-: هالطبق 'this dish'.

too_formal.feedback: MSA; 3ind is the Gulf way of having.

exercises.tip: 3ind + person ending means 'have': 3indkum is 'you (all) have'.

too_formal.feedback: MSA; bikam is the everyday price question.

exercises.tip: You can also point and say bikam without any noun.

too_formal.feedback: MSA; shi is the spoken form of shay'.

exercises.tip: shi (something) is not the same word as chaay (tea).

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: What do you recommend I get?

too_formal.feedback: MSA has 'an' before the verb; speech drops it.

exercises.tip: Two verbs in a row need no linking word: tan9a7ni aakhith.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: Is there a dish of the day?

too_formal.feedback: MSA; fii alone means 'is there'.

exercises.tip: fii is both 'there is' and the question 'is there?', by tone.

reply.english: Yes, I want this and this.

dialogue.speaker: Saeed
dialogue.english: Consider it done, and the rest?

dialogue.speaker: Layla

dialogue.speaker: Saeed
dialogue.english: Okay, do you want anything else?

dialogue.speaker: Saeed
dialogue.english: Right away, one moment.

dialogue.speaker: Saeed
dialogue.english: Sorry, it will reach you now.

response.english: Yes, I want this and this.
Sorry, it will reach you now.

lessons.culture: Gulf diners often order several dishes to share, and ordering plenty is a sign of generosity rather than greed. A waiter's abshir ("consider it done") is the standard warm way of saying yes to any request.

too_formal.feedback: MSA request; bidoon ba9al is enough.

exercises.tip: bidoon + noun is the simple way to say 'without'.

exercises.prompt: Which one means 'My order hasn't arrived yet'?

too_formal.feedback: MSA; the Gulf says lil7een + ma + verb.

exercises.tip: lil7een means 'still / yet' and is very Gulf.

too_formal.feedback: MSA; abi is what you hear.

exercises.tip: Point at the menu while saying haatha w haatha.

too_formal.feedback: Fine in MSA, but too long for the table.

exercises.tip: mashkoor (to a man) or mashkoora (to a woman) is 'thanks'.

too_formal.feedback: MSA 'ba3d' after a negative; the Gulf uses lil7een.

exercises.tip: il7een is 'now', lil7een is 'till now'.

exercises.prompt: هذا الطبق ___ وهذا حقها (haatha il6abag ___ w haatha 7aggha)

too_formal.feedback: MSA li; the Gulf uses 7ag + ending for 'belonging to'.

exercises.tip: 7ag is the Gulf 'belonging to': 7aggi, 7aggak, 7aggha.

too_formal.feedback: MSA; ziyaada khubz says it all.

exercises.tip: ziyaada means 'extra' or 'more'.

too_formal.feedback: MSA; tigdar is 'can you' in Gulf speech.

exercises.tip: The Gulf says g for ق: tigdar, not tiqdar.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: We want the same order.

too_formal.feedback: MSA nureed; the Gulf says nabi for 'we want'.

exercises.tip: nabi is the 'we' form of abi.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: Can I have a glass of water?

too_formal.item: هل يمكنني الحصول على كأس ماء
too_formal.feedback: MSA; the Gulf says mooya (or maay) for water.

exercises.tip: Water is mooya or maay in the Gulf, never maa2 in speech.

dialogue.speaker: Yousef
dialogue.english: Excuse me, the bill please.

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed

dialogue.speaker: Hamad
dialogue.english: Come on, leave it to me.

dialogue.english: Fine, next time it's on me.

dialogue.speaker: Hamad
dialogue.transliteration: tfaddal ilkart, w mumkin il faatoora?
dialogue.english: Here is the card, and can I have the receipt?

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed
dialogue.english: Of course, here you are.

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed
dialogue.english: God keep you well, we look forward to seeing you again.

response.english: No no, today it's on me.

lessons.culture: Arguing warmly over who pays is normal among Gulf friends, and the offer is 3alay (on me), often refused once before someone gives in. A small tip is common in restaurants but is not always added to the bill, so it is fine to ask.

too_formal.feedback: MSA; ilbaagi lak is the natural way to say it.

exercises.tip: ilbaagi is 'the rest', so 'the change'.

exercises.prompt: Which one offers to pay ('It's on me today')?

too_formal.feedback: Correct but plain; 3alay is the warm, common offer.

exercises.tip: 3alay means 'on me' and is the classic offer when the bill arrives.

too_formal.feedback: MSA bi-l-bi6aaqa; the Gulf says kart.

exercises.tip: cash and kart are both borrowed words used everywhere.

too_formal.feedback: Fine MSA, but the Gulf reply is 3alay.

exercises.tip: Refusing once and insisting is part of the game.

too_formal.feedback: MSA; 3alay is what a host really says.

exercises.tip: 3ala + ending: 3alay (me), 3alaak (you), 3aleeh (him).

too_formal.feedback: MSA 'am'; spoken Arabic uses walla for 'or' in questions.

exercises.tip: walla means 'or' in a question, the same walla as in coffee or tea.

too_formal.feedback: MSA; kam il7isaab is short and natural.

exercises.tip: il7isaab is the everyday word for the bill.

too_formal.feedback: MSA; mumkin alone means 'may I'.

exercises.tip: mumkin + noun is a quick polite request.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: Is there a discount today?

too_formal.feedback: MSA; fii is enough.

exercises.tip: fii + noun asks 'is there ...?'.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: The bill, please.

too_formal.feedback: Too formal; il7isaab law samaht is the everyday request.

exercises.tip: You can also just raise a hand and say il7isaab.

challenge.title: At the Restaurant
challenge.instructions: Have a full conversation at a Gulf restaurant: ask about the menu, order a drink and a dish with one preference, then ask for the bill and close the meal politely.
required_elements: Ask what the restaurant has or what it recommends
Order at least one drink and one dish, including one preference (for example no onion, extra bread or sugar level)
Ask for the bill and how much it is
Close the meal with a thank you or a compliment on the food
